items.title: 'I Feel Like Modding is Kind Of Dying' – Mass Effect 3 Multiplayer Modder on AI's Impact on the Scene
items.excerpt: Over the past few months, there's been a sort of explosion of AI in the modding scene. Whether it's mashup mods on Twitter or full decompilation done by Claude, AI is everywhere in the mod community, and it may just be killing the hobby.
items.content_text: Over the past few months, there's been an explosion of AI in the modding scene. Whether it's mashup mods on Twitter or full decompilation done by Claude , AI is everywhere in the mod community, and it could be killing the hobby. I got a chance to sit down with ME3Tweaks' Mgamerz to talk about his new Mass Effect Legendary Edition ME3 Multiplayer mod, where I asked him about how AI has affected the modding community. While he admits that Claude is very effective at modding games, it's causing an avalanche of low-effort content that's hard to sift through. And, while there has always been a range of quality for mods, the inherent difficulty of getting into a game's files and changing things was a natural filter that's slowly eroding. Mgamerz told me, "The difficulty of making mods and getting into it filtered out a lot of low-quality stuff. You see this on stuff like the Switch eShop, I've heard. It's full of slop, because there's no quality control and you can just ship whatever, and then users have to dredge through all sorts of stuff like that." Although typing in a prompt to mod your own copy of a game is one thing, the problems start to appear once you start distributing it on platforms like Nexus Mods, where you have to be mindful about how your mod will interact with other add-ons, otherwise you're likely to just break peoples' games. Mgamerz laid out that process, telling me, "In the modding community, you have an ecosystem. For example, I have my mod manager, you deploy mods through the mod manager, it runs a bunch of checks on the mods to make sure you're not going to ship something that's just going to break someone's game immediately." These AI mods can do more than just break other people's mods too — they can also make your game much harder to run if they aren't optimized properly. For example, Mgamerz says, "There's certain knowledge, like you don't put stuff in startup files because it wastes tons of memory. If you stuff everything in there, you boot the game, oh, now the game takes an extra gigabyte of memory for your single mod to work, because you didn't want to do it the proper way." It's hard to argue with the fact that these AI tools are introducing a whole new generation of gamers to modding, but it's doing so without making them go through the effort of figuring out how to make things effectively. We've already seen major modding communities pull their sites down because of this outbreak of AI modding tools that can take months of someone's hard work and spin it around into a 'working' mod after a couple of Claude prompts. And that might end up becoming the default for people who learn how to code exclusively through AI tools. When I asked Mgamerz what the pathway for people who want to get into modding these days is, his answer was grim. He told me, "Getting into [modding]? I feel like modding is kind of dying. If you come in and you're like, 'I want to just do this, no AI. I just want to cut my teeth, find the boundaries, break over them, have a difficult, challenging task,' you pretty much have to work in secret now." "Because if you essentially have an idea and someone else is like, 'Wow, that's a cool idea.' And you're like, 'Well, it's going to take me six months.' And they're like, 'I don't want to wait six months.' They can spend 20 bucks and pump this thing out in a day or two, and it'll probably work, but the user will have no understanding of how." Mgamerz understands, though, that the prevalence of these AI tools is getting a lot of people interested in modding their favorite games, and that's not a bad thing. He told me, "If you don't release the stuff that you make, I don't see any problem. You made something cool for yourself." Instead, the problem is that, if you install it without considering how it'll interact with other software, it can really bungle other peoples' projects. "Once you hand this product over to somebody else, share it with the world, suddenly it can become everybody's problem. And from my experience, everyone that vibe codes stuff, two weeks later, they're gone. They're not supporting it. So the people that stick around have to fix and deal with all of it." Ever since Claude Opus 5.5 released back in September, it feels like the modding scene has been going through a rollercoaster, and it's impossible to know where exactly it's going to land. Whether the world of Nexus Mods and publicly available GitHub forks is going to start to die down like Mgamerz thinks it will is anyone's guess. But one thing's for sure: Once The Elder Scrolls VI: Sentinel drops, modding is going to be a completely different animal than the Skyrim days, if Bethesda's next game is even moddable at all.

items.title: Godzilla Minus Zero: Where Is the Rest of Godzilla’s Rogues' Gallery?
items.excerpt: Where is the rest of Godzilla’s rogues' gallery? We take a look at Monster Island's most wanted.
items.content_text: Spoilers follow for Godzilla Minus Zero . Godzilla Minus Zero is upon us, and going by the reviews , it looks like the venerable kaiju franchise has another winner on its hands. More than 70 years after his debut, Godzilla continues to be one of the most iconic characters in cinema history. But even though Minus Zero is another strong entry for the King of the Monsters, I couldn’t help but be a little disappointed that the movie continues a frustrating trend that’s plagued the last couple decades of Godzilla movies by only featuring a handful of his monster co-stars. Specifically, King Ghidorah is the antagonist of Minus Zero, once again assuming his role as the Big G’s archenemy. Now, I love King Ghidorah, but the alien dragon takes up a lot of oxygen in Toho’s filmography, and there is a deep bench of Godzilla friends and foes who haven’t shown up in years. Let’s look into how the Godzilla franchise isn’t using its roster of monsters to their full potential. More Minus Zero Godzilla Minus Zero Ending Explained and Our Biggest Burning Questions Godzilla Minus Zero Review Minus Zero Director Talks a Potential Godzilla Threequel Minus Zero Director Had to Avoid the Urge to One-Up Godzilla Minus One Minus Zero's Big, Brutal Climax Had a Household Inspiration The Usual Suspects Although most Western audiences probably haven’t seen many of them, Toho has produced more than 30 Godzilla films since the big guy’s debut back in 1954. Godzilla may have been the sole kaiju in his first film, but starting with the sequel, Godzilla Raids Again, the first of many monster co-stars was introduced. That would be Anguirus, an ankylosaur-like kaiju who was Godzilla’s earliest adversary. Luckily, the pair made up and Anguirus became Godzilla’s most steadfast ally across the Shōwa era, consisting of the first 15 films. Many kaiju have shared the screen with Godzilla over the years, but you wouldn’t know it if you’ve only been checking out new Godzilla movies released theatrically outside Japan. Since Godzilla: Final Wars in 2004, the only Toho kaiju to have appeared in live-action are Mothra, Rodan, King Ghidorah, and Mechagodzilla. Kong doesn’t count in this context because he was created in America by Merian C. Cooper. Now those four may be among the most popular of Godzilla’s co-stars anyway, but there are many more that new films could revisit. However, since the MonsterVerse franchise apparently has to license each Toho monster individually, they often make up their own kaiju instead, like the MUTOs in the 2014 film or Skar King in Godzilla x Kong: The New Empire. Yet none of the new MonsterVerse kaiju have quite hit the same as the ones from the classic Toho films. Many kaiju have shared the screen with Godzilla over the years, but you wouldn't know it if you've only been checking out new Godzilla movies released theatrically outside Japan. King Ghidorah’s overexposure is particularly frustrating because most uses of him are good, even if he keeps hogging the spotlight. He makes a great antithesis to the big guy in Godzilla: King of the Monsters, and his Minus Zero incarnation is terrifying and awe-inspiring in equal measure. In the new film, he’s an alien who’s crash-landed in postwar Japan and started claiming the land for his own purposes — an apt metaphor for the occupying American military that hovers over the story. So we wouldn’t want director Takashi Yamazaki to have foregone Ghidorah when his appearance in Minus Zero makes sense. King Ghidorah is basically the Joker to Godzilla’s Batman: It’s awesome when they square up, but sometimes you wish they’d go with a different bad guy. It’s not like there aren’t plenty to choose from. Destroy All Monsters Over the course of Toho’s 31 live-action Godzilla films, the big guy has encountered more than two dozen other kaiju. From fellow dinosaurs to alien invaders to mechanical guardians to mutated monstrosities, Toho’s monster roster is eclectic and extensive. The Shōwa, Heisei, and Millennium eras have all added new members to the group, but the latest batch of films in the Reiwa era have left many of them on the shelf. That’s not to say the Reiwa era films are bad, mind you — Shin Godzilla and the Minus films stand up with the best of the Big G’s filmography (we’ll politely refrain from talking about the animated Netflix trilogy). Yet there’s no denying that Toho’s Reiwa films and the concurrent MonsterVerse franchise aren’t taking full advantage of the cast of characters at their disposal. Where is Gigan, the alien cyborg with scythe hands and a buzzsaw in his belly? Or Megalon, the bipedal rhinoceros beetle with drill hands who protects Seatopia, the Godzilla universe’s version of Atlantis? Or Biollante, the gargantuan plant queen that results from splicing Godzilla cells with a rose? They and many others have been eagerly awaiting a rematch with the King of the Monsters. Several other Heisei and Millennium era foes, such as Destoroyah, Orga, and Megaguirus have only made one film appearance each despite being well-liked by fans. In fact, the only live action Toho kaiju introduced after the Shōwa era to appear in more than one movie is Kiryu, a new version of Mechagodzilla constructed by the Japanese Self-Defense Forces using the bones of the 1954 Godzilla as a skeletal framework. At least one Heisei monster seems to finally be escaping purgatory: SpaceGodzilla, who according to a Writer’s Guild of America registration , is set to appear in the upcoming Godzilla x Kong: Supernova. All well and good, but I hope the rest of Godzilla’s rogues' gallery is being considered for more appearances in the future, especially given how anxious fans are to see more of their favorite monsters, and the success the Godzilla franchise has enjoyed on multiple fronts over the past several years. Now is the perfect time to reintroduce the rest of Toho’s monsters to international audiences. Unleash the Beasts Some fans have argued that Toho exclusively focusing on their most popular monsters like Mothra, Rodan, and King Ghidorah is a sound business move because they’re the most recognizable Godzilla co-stars to audiences outside Japan. That may be true, but it doesn’t account for how Godzilla’s wider cast has been kept alive in the cultural imagination by expanded universe media. Comics, animated shows, and a legion of video games have often utilized monsters that the films have neglected, with the Pipeworks trilogy of fighting games — starting with Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee — introducing an entire generation of younger gamers to the Big G’s friends and foes. The enduring popularity of those games as a nostalgic touchstone resulted in DAMM recently being reborn with its Remastered edition. The hunger from fans for other kaiju co-stars has even expressed itself in humorous ways. When the first teaser for Godzilla Minus Zero dropped in April, many fans joked that the blue gravity beams used by Ghidorah were actually going to belong to “Gravity Anguirus,” a hypothetical version of the character with new gravity manipulation powers. Gravity Anguirus may be a meme, but the way the joke spread across Godzilla fandom speaks to how much the people yearn to see Godzilla’s best friend back on the big screen. The poor guy must be feeling left out watching Godzilla and Kong go on adventures together. And as a personal note, what do I have to do to get my incompetent son Ebirah the giant lobster back in circulation? At the end of the day, the Godzilla franchise is in a great spot. He’s got two successful movie series running simultaneously, Legacy of Monsters appears to be a hit on AppleTV+, and Destroy All Monsters Remastered has reignited Godzilla’s relevance in the gaming space. Toho’s stewardship of the series in the modern day is to be commended... but if there’s one place with room for improvement, it’s opening the door so the rest of their characters can share the spotlight. Godzilla, Mothra, Rodan, and King Ghidorah are all fantastic monsters; I’d just like to see the rest of their friends join them on the playground. items.title: Gundam Assemble: Hands-On With Mobile Suit Gundam’s Miniatures Tabletop Game
items.excerpt: Get a closer look at the Gundam Assemble Starter Set.
items.content_text: The storied Mobile Suit Gundam series makes another venture into the tabletop world with Gundam Assemble, a new miniatures game experience. In fact, this new game was revealed alongside the Gundam Card Game as a visual companion, so fans got hit with a fun one-two punch of new game teases. Gundam Assemble is available for the first time this fall, with more expansion packs and sets already prepared to release into early next year. After a good chunk of time with the starter set, this game is shaping up to be a fun bite-size brawl compared to some of the other miniature games out there right now. Arguably one of the biggest barriers of entry to miniature wargames is the building and painting aspect. If building is your biggest concern, have no fear with Gundam Assemble. Just like the gunpla that the series is known for, Gundam Assemble features pieces that you cut out and snap into place. Granted, the pieces are a lot smaller in comparison to regular gunpla, but it’s simplified, needing only a handful of parts to complete a mini Gundam unit. I suggest using proper cutting tools since these are miniatures and there’s less room for error. They look good though, showcasing a decent amount of detail for miniature versions of what fans are familiar with. Like other modern miniatures, assembly has been made a lot easier by simply snapping parts together as instructed, but it loses the customization that players may prefer with particular sets of miniature games. Instead, we see different variants or poses of Gundam units across the different releases. For instance, the RX-78-2 Gundam in the starter set features a beam saber attack, but the variant in the Paint Pack has the mech unit brandishing a beam rifle. Although not ideal for those that want a little bit of personal touch to their creations, it does make it easier for beginners (or even impatient players like myself) to jump right into painting and the gameplay soon after. Painting miniatures is not for the faint of heart, and Gundam Assemble isn’t any easier with all the tiny details, from the weapons to the mech head pieces. And if you’re a perfectionist, you’ll be spending more time painting than even playing the game. With that said, the mech units in the Gundam universe are fairly straightforward to paint with the mostly monochrome looks with embellishments littered about. Thankfully, there’s no skin or flesh color to deal with while painting Gundam units, which can be difficult to do properly. As long as you start off with a primer, you can save a bit of time, especially with units like the RX-78-2 or the Wing Gundam Zero. For me, I like to keep painting fairly simple because I just don’t have as much free time nowadays. And I care more about the gameplay than the arts and crafts of it all anyway. With that said, I do still want to make things look somewhat cool and clean compared to what I did as a 12-year-old painting Black Templar Space Marines because it was one of the easier chapters to paint. On the flip side, I’d prefer to skip painting altogether if possible, and that’s how I got into other miniature games like HeroClix and Star Wars X-Wing – where the minis were already painted. You can also just not paint the minis, but the extra effort does make for a better experience. The starter set even has a painting guide section in its instruction manual if you’re new to the hobby. Other than having some specific paints available like the Gundam Assemble Paint Pack, it’s also fine to use any water-based acrylic model paint and mix colors as need be. That’s how Char’s Zaku’s colors turned out when some friends and I had a dedicated paint day for some of these minis. Overall, painting is much easier now and it saves a ton of time if you do a bit of research before getting started. As I mentioned, I care mostly about the gameplay when it comes to miniature games, and Gundam Assemble’s matches are surprisingly a smooth experience. I’m not in the miniatures tabletop scene constantly, but I dabble with some casual games every now and then like Marvel United. The hardest part is finding a buddy or group willing to learn the complex game mechanics and dedicating time and space to matches. It’s been kind of a sore spot for me and my friends lately, always talking about wanting to play Warhammer 40K Kill Team , but never fully committing because we still want to properly build and paint. With Gundam Assemble, it’s easier to get games going because you only really need six mech units versus a multitude of grunts to fill up a squad or army on either side. Although there are still a lot of tokens for various effects and objectives, the most important feature that makes turn-taking smooth is the Gundam Assemble timeline. It consists of ten rounds equaling one phase. On the timeline, players have their mech units’ tokens slotted into specific spots to help track each unit’s turn. For example, the Gundam Vidar has a timeline start number of one compared to RX-78-2’s timeline start number two. This means that Gundam Vidar places its token on round one of the timeline at setup, signifying that it takes its turn first before moving to round two, where RX-78-2’s token sits. As units make certain actions, their unit token moves down the timeline. So depending on what your mech unit does, they could be waiting a long time to act again. Seeing which mech is next in line does give an extra layer of strategy similar to turn-based video games like Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 or Digimon Survive . It’s nice to have the timeline set to the side of the map and away from the battlefield where token placements can get out of hand. In a common scenario, players play through two phases or 20 rounds, trying to collect as many victory points as possible through various means. Scoring victory points ranges from rescuing/destroying garrisons to defeating a mech unit or holding objective points at the end of each phase. Each mech unit’s turn consists of a few possible options: advance, primary action, command abilities, and tactics cards. Advance is simply movement, and units can move up to three hexes in any direction. Although, when it comes to moving up a level of terrain, it costs two hexes of movement. There’s no terrain penalty going down a level, and units with a Hover ability ignore terrain penalties all together. Primary actions move the unit token down the timeline and includes options like attack, dash, energize, and rescue. Attacks on the unit cards have specific timeline costs. So if the RX-78-2’s Beam Saber attack has a timeline of three, the Gundam’s token moves down the timeline three rounds after using this specific attack. The other three primary actions normally cost two timeline rounds. Dash is an option to move two hexes further. In Char’s Zaku’s case, dashes can also deal damage with his Char Kick ability. Next is energize, which gives a unit an energy token so they can use certain abilities later in the game. And the last primary action is rescue, which can be used to rescue friendly garrison tokens on the battlefield for victory points. Some units benefit from rescuing garrisons like the RX-78-2, which has a command ability that increases its strength by one for every garrison rescued. Speaking of command abilities, that’s another option available during a mech unit’s turn that’s printed on the unit card. These command abilities usually have an energy cost and/or specific requirement, so plan accordingly. And finally there are tactics cards, which can be used up to once a turn before being discarded. Players start off with three tactics cards but eventually draw more after a phase ends. These are one-time use, ranging from repairing a mech unit to using an entirely new attack or countering an enemy unit. It seems like a lot for one turn, but at most times, players are mainly just advancing and using a primary action as options on the battlefield start to dwindle. Of course, we have to talk about the combat in a Gundam miniatures game. Since games are typically 3v3 mech units, the battlefield is not too cluttered with miniatures, so entering combat gameplay is fairly quick in the opening turns as they each get deployed onto the battlefield and disperse towards various objectives. When enemy units are in range, the player’s unit can choose one of two attacks printed on their card or possibly an attack Tactics card. Each attack has a strength number and that signals how many 10-sided dice to use to calculate hits, criticals, and damage. Four and greater is a hit which equals one damage, and nines or tens are critical hits that activate the attack’s crit effect – whether it’s additional damage or a negative effect that hinders a unit’s capabilities. Unlike other games, Gundam Assemble doesn’t have defensive rolls like saving throws, so its damage calculation can be fairly easy. Instead, defenses can be used in the form of Shield tokens that a unit can pick up by chance or applied via a command ability or tactics card. Shield tokens are passive bonuses that nullify one hit per token equipped, and become exhausted or deactivated until the start of that mech unit’s turn. For example, the Gundam Barbatos Lupus Rex’s Tail Blade attack attempts to deal six damage to Gundam Vidar, but the defending unit has two Shield tokens equipped. Instead of taking six damage, Gundam Vidar only takes four and the two Shield tokens are flipped over to signify being used. If another unit comes along to attack the Gundam Vidar before it reactivates its Shield tokens, the tokens will not defend two hits of damage. This, alongside some abilities or tactics cards that can nullify or lessen damage, keep combat rolls fairly quick and seamless. There’s no need to calculate a multitude of faction bonuses or if a unit is concealed or aiming like in other miniature wargames so far. The only other consideration when attacking is accuracy, which can be altered by elevation or special terrain like water. When a mech unit is eventually defeated, the winning player gains victory points as noted on the enemy unit’s card. Then the enemy unit’s token on the timeline is moved two spaces ahead when it can redeploy again after ‘repairs’ have been made. Any upgrades or energy accumulated stay with the defeated mech unit until it deploys again. One other thing worth mentioning when it comes to any miniatures games is the price. After all, these detailed minis are a step above acrylic or cardboard standees or tokens, and it can get overwhelming when deciding which units to collect. The Gundam Assemble Starter Set 01 will run you about $35, which isn’t that much more than a HG gunpla kit, depending on the model. Considering a starter set of Warhammer 40K Kill Team can run you about $118 or a Star Wars Legion starter at about $99, Gundam Assemble is much easier on the wallet. I know my mom would’ve appreciated that when I first got into Warhammer 40K back in the day. With that said, there is a Deluxe Starter Set for Gundam Assemble at about $100, which contains double the minis of a regular starter. And if you’re feeling the itch, there are expansion packs featuring fan favorites that can run you $40. Gundam Assemble’s gameplay is a nice blend of objective-based scoring while also having the option to just all-out attack enemy units for their VP rewards. It’s the balance of managing both strategies to your units’ best abilities that determines who is the better tactician. Between the easy builds that gunpla and miniature fans are familiar with to the fairly quick instances of combat and timeline management, the barrier to entry is slightly more beginner-friendly than other starter sets in the miniature wargame landscape. Not to mention, the price isn’t too bad for Gundam fans interested in a new tabletop experience, or those looking to venture into miniature games for the first time. For more Gundam, check out our hands-on impressions of the Gundam Card Game or our interview with the Director of Gundam RG XARX-Zero, Kenji Kamiyama . Mike Mamon is a Syndication & Digital Specialist at IGN, devil fruit user, and world-renown JoJo poser. Let's chat anime or TCGs on Bluesky @xpmnms.bsky.social

items.title: World of Warcraft Forever World First Level 60 Character Hits Cap Three Days After Launch
items.excerpt: World of Warcraft Forever World First Level 60 Character Hits Cap Three Days After Launch
items.content_text: World of Warcraft Forever is all about taking your time and exploring the world, rather than rushing to the endgame. But, despite the Forever team's insistence on taking your time and making friends, a WoW Forever player has already hit level 60. Team JokerD, led by the eponymous streamer was the first team of characters to hit level 60, and the team was made up entirely of Undead characters and one Troll. The Undead race was important there, because Blizzard changed the Cannibalize ability to help you regenerate mana, which meant there was little to no downtime between massive pulls. I spent some time watching the streams of these speedrunners, and they'd gather entire groups of mobs to nuke them down with AoE abilities. JokerD's claim to fame was being the world's first level 60 when World of Warcraft Classic launched back in 2019, so it's not super suprising that his team was the first to hit max level in Forever. There was plenty of competition this time around, but JokerD's team was pretty far ahead of the fray throughout the entire race. Even at the time of writing, the second place character who's not part of JokerD's team is Ksuper Worldfirst, who is still level 53. However, while it's cool that these players have been able to hit max level already, there's not much of a reason to rush to endgame right now. The first raids, Barrow Deeps, Hyjal Summit and Onyxia's Lair, don't open until December 9, so players hitting level cap this weekend might find it hard to find what they should do next. When I interviewed WoW Forever principal game designer Kris Zierhut , he made it pretty clear that Blizzard intends players to level multiple characters, and reinforced that leveling is a major part of the game. So, if you do manage to make it to level 60 super early and you run out of content before raids open, it might be worth it to start another character and take a different path to max level. WoW Forever also had an extremely smooth launch , and was largely free of any major server problems. But, then again, Blizzard later came out and bragged that the game was running on more than 200TB of RAM, so it'd be a little concerning if the servers still buckled under the weight of players trying to log in.

items.title: Robert Pattinson Reportedly Screen-Tested for 007 in James Bond 26
items.excerpt: Robert Pattinson reportedly screen-tested for the role of 007 in James Bond 26. Lex Luthor actor Nicholas Hoult has also emerged as a contender for the role of Bond.
items.content_text: Robert Pattinson reportedly screen-tested for the role of 007 in James Bond 26 . "The screen tests are said to have occurred the weekend of Oct. 24," according to The Hollywood Reporter . "THR previously reported that four, possibly five actors were in the mix but only three names surfaced at the time." Those three named actors are Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor . THR also said Lex Luthor actor Nicholas Hoult has emerged as a contender for the role of Bond. This wouldn't be the first time Hoult and Pattinson have vied for the same high-profile franchise role. Hoult was the runner-up for the role of Batman in Matt Reeves’ 2022 film, which Pattinson won. Meanwhile, Variety claims that "Harry Styles has had discussions about the part, and Theo James also hasn’t been ruled out." It’s unusual but not unheard of for an actor to lead two big franchises at the same time. Harrison Ford played Han Solo and Indiana Jones in the same era, later adding Jack Ryan to the mix. Robert Downey Jr. starred in the Sherlock Holmes films while anchoring the MCU as Iron Man. Pattinson recently worked with James Bond 26 director Denis Villeneuve on Dune: Part 3. The Bond screen tests took place in London where Pattinson is currently filming The Batman: Part 2. At 40 years old, Pattinson is older than the three other named 007 contenders and Hoult, who are all 36 years old. As someone who launched to global fame with the Twilight films, Pattinson is a far cry from the "fresh face" that producers were reportedly looking to cast at one point. For more 007 coverage, take a look back at how the media has reacted to the casting of the James Bond actors . What do you think of Robert Pattinson possibly being both Batman and James Bond? Let us know in the comments.
